extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemakers, regulatory attorneys, and public commenters interested in administrative law and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply post‑Loper Bright administrative‑law standards relevant to agency rulemaking and notice‑and‑comment practice, especially whether regulations match the statute's "best reading." Useful for drafting, reviewing, or commenting on federal rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Chevron deference; courts must determine the statute's best interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency interpretations of statutes and agency actions that rely on them do not receive any judicial deference. The reviewing court itself must determine the best interpretation of a statute and then assess whether the challenged [agency action] is authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (articulated in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo) means courts will exercise independent judgment rather than deferring to an agency's "permissible" reading. Practically, commenters and agencies should frame arguments around whether the agency action is authorized by the statute's best reading rather than arguing that the agency's interpretation is merely reasonable or permissible under Chevron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best‑reading test for statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The "best reading" of a statute is determined by reference to the language itself, the specific context in which that language is used, and the broader context of the statute as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or defending a regulation, analyses should focus on textual reading, the provision's specific context, and the statute's broader structure and purpose (citing Valladares v. Ray and Robinson v. Shell Oil as supporting interpretive authorities). Arguments that rely on ambiguity + agency deference are no longer dispositive; instead show how the statute's text and context point to the single best meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must act within the statutory authority conferred by Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: When a particular statute delegates authority to an agency consistent with constitutional limits, courts must respect the delegation, while ensuring the agency acts within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under post‑Loper Bright APA review, parties and agencies should evaluate whether the challenged regulation or action falls within the specific boundaries of the statutory delegation. Demonstrate (or dispute) that Congress authorized the precise regulatory choice rather than relying on general notions of agency expertise or policy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should review and rescind regulations not based on the statute's best reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Orders and agency reviews direct departments to review and rescind unlawful regulations that are "based on anything other than the best reading of the underlying statutory authority." Agencies are revising or rescinding regulations to conform more closely with statutory text and the post‑Loper Bright standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulewriters should proactively reassess existing rules (especially those originally justified under Chevron) and either (a) revise explanations and rule text to show alignment with the statute's best reading, or (b) propose rescission if no statutory foundation exists. Commenters may use this criterion to press for rescission of rules lacking textual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may update prior interpretations to align with the best reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in Loper Bright changed the proposition that agencies may update their interpretations of the statutes that they implement, even interpretations previously upheld by a court as reasonable under Chevron, particularly to align the agency's interpretation with the best reading of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies can and should revise long‑standing interpretations where a renewed textual analysis supports a different view; rulemakings that update agency interpretation should show why the new reading is the best reading (text, context, structure). Commenters should address both the reasonableness of the new reading under the best‑reading framework and any reliance interests or retroactivity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate regulatory requirements for a statutory foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific regulatory requirements must be justified by the statute's text and structure; where the statute does not authorize a requirement, the agency should remove it. (Example: the Department tentatively finds WIOA does not authorize affirmative outreach.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or commenting, analyze whether the statute's text authorizes the particular regulatory mandate (not just whether it is a sensible policy). Where statutory authorization is thin or absent, argue for removal or narrowing of the regulatory requirement on textualist best‑reading grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination of prior case law or agency rules that relied on Chevron
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions and regulations whose legal foundation relied on Chevron deference are subject to reexamination and criticism post‑Loper Bright; commenters have argued such decisions are invalid because they "relied on Chevron."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In litigation, rulemaking comments, or agency reviews, parties should flag precedents or regulations that depended on Chevron reasoning and explain why the underlying statutory interpretation must be reanalyzed under the best‑reading standard. Agencies and courts may no longer treat Chevron‑based conclusions as authoritative without independent textual analysis.
